cor-basis-existence.title: Existence of Bases
cor-basis-existence.html: Every finite-dimensional vector space has a basis.

cor-span-intersection.title: Span as an Intersection
cor-span-intersection.html: Let V be a vector space and S⊆V. Let U be the set of all subspaces U of V with S⊆U. Then span(S)=⋂U∈UU.

def-additive-inverse-notation.title: Notation for the Additive Inverse
def-additive-inverse-notation.html: Let V be a vector space over F and v∈V. The unique additive inverse of v is denoted −v. For u,v∈V we write u−v:=u+(−v).

def-basis.title: Basis
def-basis.html:
Let V be a vector space over F. A basis of V is a list (v1,…,vn) of vectors in V such that

  1. (v1,…,vn) is linearly independent, and
  2. (v1,…,vn) spans V, that is, span(v1,…,vn)=V.

We usually name a basis with a calligraphic letter, B=(v1,…,vn), and call n its length. The plural of basis is bases.

def-complexification.title: Complexification
def-complexification.html: Let V be a vector space over R. The complexification of V is the set VC:=V×V with addition and scalar multiplication by C defined, for all (u,v),(u′,v′)∈VC and a,b∈R, by (u,v)+(u′,v′):=(u+u′,v+v′),(a+bi)(u,v):=(au−bv,av+bu). We write u+iv for (u,v), and u for (u,0).

def-coordinates.title: Coordinates
def-coordinates.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of a vector space V over F, and let v∈V. The unique scalars a1,…,an with v=a1v1+⋯+anvn are the coordinates of v with respect to B. The column [v]B:=(a1⋮an)∈Fn is the coordinate vector of v with respect to B.

def-countable.title: Countable Set
def-countable.html: A set A is countable if A=∅ or there is a surjective function N→A. Otherwise A is uncountable.

def-dimension.title: Dimension
def-dimension.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F. The dimension of V over F, written dimF⁡V or simply dim⁡V, is the length of any basis of V.

def-direct-sum.title: Direct Sum
def-direct-sum.html: Let U1,…,Uk be subspaces of a vector space V over F. The sum U1+⋯+Uk is direct if every vector v∈U1+⋯+Uk can be written in exactly one way as v=u1+⋯+ukwith ui∈Ui for each i. In that case we write the sum as U1⊕⋯⊕Uk. We write V=U1⊕⋯⊕Uk to mean that V=U1+⋯+Uk and the sum is direct.

def-finite-dimensional.title: Finite-Dimensional
def-finite-dimensional.html: A vector space V over F is finite-dimensional if some finite list of vectors in V spans V. Otherwise V is infinite-dimensional.

def-linear-combination.title: Linear Combination
def-linear-combination.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let (v1,…,vk) be a list of vectors in V, where k≥0. A linear combination of (v1,…,vk) is a vector of the form a1v1+a2v2+⋯+akvk,where a1,…,ak∈F. The scalars ai are the coefficients of the combination. A linear combination of the empty list is, by convention, the empty sum 0.

def-linear-independence.title: Linear Independence
def-linear-independence.html: Let V be a vector space over F and let (v1,…,vk) be a list of vectors in V, where k≥0. The list is linearly independent (over F) if, for all a1,…,ak∈F, a1v1+a2v2+⋯+akvk=0⟹a1=a2=⋯=ak=0. The list is linearly dependent if it is not linearly independent: that is, if there exist a1,…,ak∈F, not all zero, with a1v1+⋯+akvk=0. Such an equation is a linear relation among the vectors. The empty list is linearly independent.

def-partial-order.title: Partial Order, Chain, Upper Bound, Maximal Element
def-partial-order.title_html: Partial Order, Chain, Upper Bound, Maximal Element
def-partial-order.html:
Let P be a set. A partial order on P is a relation ≤ on P (@def-relation) such that, for all p,q,r∈P:

  1. p≤p (reflexive);
  2. if p≤q and q≤p, then p=q (antisymmetric);
  3. if p≤q and q≤r, then p≤r (transitive).

Let (P,≤) be a partially ordered set.

  • A chain in P is a subset C⊆P such that for all p,q∈C, p≤q or q≤p.
  • An upper bound of a subset C⊆P is an element u∈P with c≤u for every c∈C.
  • A maximal element of P is an element m∈P such that no p∈P satisfies m≤p and p≠m.

def-restriction-of-scalars.title: Subfield, Restriction of Scalars, Degree
def-restriction-of-scalars.html:
Let L be a field. A subfield of L is a subset K⊆L that contains 0 and 1 and is closed under addition, multiplication, negatives, and inverses of non-zero elements.

Let K be a subfield of L, and let V be a vector space over L. Keeping the addition of V and using scalar multiplication only for scalars in K makes V a vector space over K. We say V is obtained by restriction of scalars.

In particular L itself, a vector space over L, is a vector space over K. If it is finite-dimensional, its dimension is the degree [L:K]:=dimK⁡L.

def-span.title: Span
def-span.html:
Let V be a vector space over F.

  • The span of a list (v1,…,vk) of vectors in V is the set of all its linear combinations: span(v1,…,vk)={a1v1+⋯+akvk:a1,…,ak∈F}.
  • The span of a subset S⊆V, possibly infinite, is the set of all vectors that are linear combinations of some finite list of vectors in S: span(S)={a1s1+⋯+aksk:k≥0, s1,…,sk∈S, a1,…,ak∈F}.

In particular span()=span(∅)={0}. When the field matters we write spanF.

def-spanning-set.title: Spanning List, Spanning Set
def-spanning-set.html: Let V be a vector space over F. A list (v1,…,vk) in V spans V, or is a spanning list of V, if span(v1,…,vk)=V. A subset S⊆V spans V, or is a spanning set of V, if span(S)=V.

def-subspace.title: Subspace
def-subspace.html:
Let V be a vector space over F. A subset U⊆V is a subspace of V if

  • u+w∈U and au∈U for all u,w∈U and a∈F, so that the operations of V restrict to functions U×U→U and F×U→U; and
  • U, with these restricted operations, is a vector space over F.

def-sum-of-subspaces.title: Sum of Subspaces
def-sum-of-subspaces.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let U and W be subspaces of V. The sum of U and W is the subset U+W:={u+w:u∈U and w∈W}. More generally, for subspaces U1,…,Uk of V (with k≥1), their sum is U1+⋯+Uk:={u1+⋯+uk:ui∈Ui for each i=1,…,k}.

def-vector-space.title: Vector Space
def-vector-space.html:
Let F be a field. A vector space over F is a set V together with two functions +:V×V→V, (u,v)↦u+v,⋅:F×V→V, (a,v)↦av, called addition and scalar multiplication, such that the following axioms hold.

  1. u+v=v+u for all u,v∈V.
  2. (u+v)+w=u+(v+w) for all u,v,w∈V.
  3. There exists an element 0∈V such that v+0=v for every v∈V.
  4. For every v∈V there exists an element v′∈V such that v+v′=0.
  5. a(u+v)=au+av for all a∈F and u,v∈V.
  6. (a+b)v=av+bv for all a,b∈F and v∈V.
  7. a(bv)=(ab)v for all a,b∈F and v∈V.
  8. 1v=v for every v∈V, where 1 is the identity element of F.

def-vectors-scalars.title: Vectors and Scalars
def-vectors-scalars.html: Let V be a vector space over F. The elements of V are called vectors, and the elements of F are called scalars. The element 0 in (VS3) is a zero vector of V, and an element v′ as in (VS4) is an additive inverse of v.

exr-changing-the-field-c1.html:
Let W⊆Cn be a subspace over R.

  1. Prove that W is a subspace over C if and only if iw∈W for every w∈W.
  2. Deduce that if W is a subspace over C, then dimR⁡W is even.
  3. Show that W0={(z,z―):z∈C}⊆C2 is a subspace over R of even real dimension that is not a subspace over C. So the converse of (b) fails.

exr-changing-the-field-c2.title: C2: A Tower of Degree Four
exr-changing-the-field-c2.title_html: C2: A Tower of Degree Four
exr-changing-the-field-c2.html:
Let V={x+y3:x,y∈Q(2)}⊆R.

  1. Prove that 3∉Q(2).
  2. Regard R as a vector space over its subfield Q(2). Prove that V is a subspace with basis (1,3).
  3. Deduce that dimQ⁡V=4, with basis (1,2,3,6).

Hint for (a): square both sides, and argue with remainders on division by 3.

exr-dimension-a1.title: A1
exr-dimension-a1.html:
1. State the Steinitz Exchange Theorem.
  2. True or false: dim⁡R[x]≤3=3. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: in a vector space of dimension 3, every spanning list of length 3 is a basis. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: M2(R) contains a linearly independent list of length 5. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if U and W are subspaces of R4 with dim⁡U=dim⁡W=2, then U=W. Justify your answer.
  6. What are dimC⁡C2 and dimR⁡C2?

exr-dimension-b1.title: B1: Dimension and a Basis of a Subspace
exr-dimension-b1.title_html: B1: Dimension and a Basis of a Subspace
exr-dimension-b1.html:
Find a basis and the dimension of each subspace.

  1. U1={(x1,x2,x3,x4)∈R4:x1+x2=0 and x3−x4=0}.
  2. U2={A∈M3(R):trA=0}.
  3. U3={p∈R[x]≤3:p(1)=p(−1)=0}.

exr-dimension-b2.title: B2: Extending to a Basis of \nR^4
exr-dimension-b2.title_html: B2: Extending to a Basis of R4
exr-dimension-b2.html: Show that ((1,1,0,0),(0,1,1,0)) is linearly independent, and extend it to a basis of R4 using vectors from the standard basis.

exr-dimension-b3.title: B3: Count Instead of Check
exr-dimension-b3.html: Show that (1,x−1,(x−1)2) is a basis of R[x]≤2. Hence find the coordinate vector of x2 with respect to this basis.

exr-dimension-c1.title: C1: Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
exr-dimension-c1.html:
Let n≥1. For a field F, let U+ and U− be the subspaces of symmetric and of skew-symmetric matrices in Mn(F) (@def-symmetric-matrix): U+={A:AT=A} and U−={A:AT=−A}.

  1. For F=R, prove that dim⁡U+=n(n+1)2.
  2. For F=R, prove that dim⁡U−=n(n−1)2.
  3. For F=F2, show that U−=U+, and find its dimension. Which step of (b) fails?

exr-dimension-c2.title: C2: A complex space viewed over the reals
exr-dimension-c2.title_html: C2: A complex space viewed over the reals
exr-dimension-c2.html:
Let V be a vector space over C with dimC⁡V=n. Restricting the scalars to real numbers makes V a vector space over R. Prove that dimR⁡V=2n.

Hint: start from a basis (v1,…,vn) over C, and consider the vectors ivk.

exr-dimension-c3.title: C3: Counting Elements over a Finite Field
exr-dimension-c3.title_html: C3: Counting Elements over a Finite Field
exr-dimension-c3.html:
Let p be a prime.

  1. Let V be a vector space over Fp with dim⁡V=k. Prove that V has exactly pk elements.
  2. Deduce that no vector space over F2 has exactly 6 elements.
  3. Let K be a finite field that contains Fp, with the same addition and multiplication. Explain why K is a finite-dimensional vector space over Fp, and deduce that K has pk elements for some integer k≥1.

Hint: for (a), use coordinates.

exr-independence-a1.title: A1
exr-independence-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a list (v1,…,vk) in a vector space over F to be linearly independent, and what it means for it to be linearly dependent.
  2. Determine whether the following statement is true: “a list of vectors is linearly dependent if and only if one of its vectors is a scalar multiple of another.” Justify your answer.
  3. Is the empty list linearly independent? Is the list (0)?
  4. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if (v1,v2,v3) is linearly dependent, then v3∈span(v1,v2).” Justify your answer.
  5. To prove that a list of functions R→R is independent, what does “=0” mean, and what is a standard way to extract scalar equations?

exr-independence-b1.title: B1: Independent or Not?
exr-independence-b1.html:
Determine which of the following lists are linearly independent. Justify your answer.

  1. ((1,0,2),(0,1,1),(1,1,3)) in R3.
  2. ((1,1,0),(0,1,1),(1,0,1)) in R3.
  3. (x2+1,x2−1,x) in R[x].
  4. ((1001),(0110),(1111)) in M2(R).
  5. (f,g) in RR, where f(t)=et and g(t)=e2t.

exr-independence-b2.title: B2: A Parameter
exr-independence-b2.html: For which t∈R is the list ((1,t),(t,1)) in R2 linearly independent? Justify your answer.

exr-independence-b3.title: B3: Sub-Lists
exr-independence-b3.html:
A sub-list of (v1,…,vk) is a list (vi1,…,vim) with 1≤i1<i2<⋯<im≤k.

  1. Prove that every sub-list of a linearly independent list is linearly independent.
  2. Deduce that if some sub-list of a list is linearly dependent, then the whole list is linearly dependent.

exr-independence-c1.title: C1: Sums of Pairs, and the Field \nF_2
exr-independence-c1.title_html: C1: Sums of Pairs, and the Field F2
exr-independence-c1.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and (u,v,w) a linearly independent list in V.

  1. Suppose F=R. Prove that (u+v,v+w,w+u) is linearly independent.
  2. Suppose F=F2. Prove that (u+v,v+w,w+u) is linearly dependent, and give an example of an independent list (u,v,w) over F2, so that the statement is not vacuous.
  3. Which property of R did (a) use that F2 lacks? Deduce that (a) holds over every field in which 1+1≠0.

exr-independence-c2.title: C2: Adding a Vector outside the Span
exr-independence-c2.title_html: C2: Adding a Vector outside the Span
exr-independence-c2.html: Let (v1,…,vk) be a linearly independent list in V, and let v∈V with v∉span(v1,…,vk). Prove that (v1,…,vk,v) is linearly independent. Give an example showing that the hypothesis v∉span(v1,…,vk) cannot be dropped.

exr-independence-c3.title: C3: 1, \sqrt 2, \sqrt 3 over \nQ
exr-independence-c3.title_html: C3: 1,2,3 over Q
exr-independence-c3.html:
Regard R as a vector space over Q. Prove that the list (1,2,3) is linearly independent over Q. Is it linearly independent over R?

Hint: you may use without proof that 3 and 6 are irrational (the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational adapts). Isolate one square root and square.

exr-infinite-dimensional-a1.title: A1
exr-infinite-dimensional-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for an arbitrary subset S of a vector space V to be a basis of V.
  2. State Zorn’s Lemma, including the meaning of “chain” and “upper bound”.
  3. True or false: {ei:i∈N} is a basis of FN. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: every linearly independent subset of an infinite-dimensional space is infinite. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: in a partially ordered set, a maximal element m satisfies p≤m for every p. Justify your answer.

exr-infinite-dimensional-b1.title: B1: Finitely Supported Sequences
exr-infinite-dimensional-b1.html:
Let F(N)⊆FN be the set of sequences with only finitely many non-zero entries.

  1. Prove that F(N) is a subspace of FN.
  2. Prove that {ei:i∈N} is a basis of F(N).

exr-infinite-dimensional-b2.title: B2: Exponentials Are Independent
exr-infinite-dimensional-b2.html:
For k∈N let fk∈RR be fk(x)=ekx. Prove that {fk:k∈N} is linearly independent. Hence deduce that RR is infinite-dimensional.

Hint: divide by the fastest-growing term.

exr-infinite-dimensional-b3.title: B3: Continuous Functions
exr-infinite-dimensional-b3.html:
Let C[0,1] be the space of continuous functions [0,1]→R. Prove that C[0,1] is infinite-dimensional.

Hint: use “tent” functions supported on disjoint intervals, and choose good points.

exr-infinite-dimensional-c1.title: C1: Complements in Any Dimension
exr-infinite-dimensional-c1.html:
Let U be a subspace of a vector space V, of any dimension. Prove that there is a subspace W of V with V=U⊕W, that is, every v∈V can be written uniquely as u+w with u∈U, w∈W.

Hint: @thm-basis-extension-general.

exr-infinite-dimensional-c2.title: C2: Bases of \nR over \nQ Are Uncountable
exr-infinite-dimensional-c2.title_html: C2: Bases of R over Q Are Uncountable
exr-infinite-dimensional-c2.html:
1. Let A0,A1,A2,… be countable sets. Prove that ⋃n∈NAn is countable. (You may use the axiom of choice.)
  2. Let V be a vector space over Q with a countable basis. Prove that V is countable.
  3. Deduce that every basis of R over Q is uncountable.

Hint: for (b), write V as a union of spans of finite lists.

exr-span-a1.title: A1
exr-span-a1.html:
1. Define the span of a subset S of a vector space V. What is span(∅), and why?
  2. Determine whether the following statement is true: “for a subset S⊆V, span(S)=S if and only if S is a subspace of V.” Justify your answer.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if span(S)=span(T), then S=T.” Justify your answer.
  4. Is the zero vector in the span of every list? Is it in the span of the empty list?
  5. State what it means for V to be finite-dimensional, and name the quantity used to show that F[x] is not.

exr-span-b1.title: B1: Membership in a Span
exr-span-b1.html:
Determine whether each vector lies in the given span. If it does, write it as a linear combination. Justify your answer.

  1. (2,−1,5) and (3,4,1), in span((1,1,0),(0,1,1))⊆R3.
  2. 2x2−3x+1 and x2+x+1, in span(x2−x,x−1)⊆R[x].

exr-span-b2.title: B2: Two Lists with the Same Span
exr-span-b2.title_html: B2: Two Lists with the Same Span
exr-span-b2.html: Prove that span((1,1,0),(0,1,1))=span((1,2,1),(1,0,−1)) in R3.

exr-span-b3.title: B3: Spans in \nR^3, Geometrically
exr-span-b3.title_html: B3: Spans in R3, Geometrically
exr-span-b3.html:
Describe each span as the origin, a line through the origin, a plane through the origin (give an equation), or all of R3. Justify your answer.

  1. span((1,2,3)).
  2. span((1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,0)).
  3. span((1,−1,0),(0,1,−1)).
  4. span((0,0,0)).

exr-span-c1.title: C1: Spans of Intersections and Unions
exr-span-c1.title_html: C1: Spans of Intersections and Unions
exr-span-c1.html:
Let S,T be subsets of a vector space V.

  1. Prove that span(S∩T)⊆span(S)∩span(T).
  2. Give an example in R2 where the inclusion in (a) is strict.
  3. Prove that span(S∪T)={s+t:s∈span(S), t∈span(T)}.

Hint for (c): in a combination of vectors of S∪T, sort the terms into two groups.

exr-span-c2.title: C2: The Span Depends on the Field
exr-span-c2.title_html: C2: The Span Depends on the Field
exr-span-c2.html:
The set C2 is a vector space over C. With the same addition, and scalar multiplication restricted to real scalars, it is also a vector space over R, by @exr-vector-spaces-c3: every axiom holds for all complex scalars, so in particular for real ones.

  1. Show that ((1,0),(0,1)) spans C2 over C.
  2. Explain why ((1,0),(0,1)) does not span C2 over R.
  3. Find a finite list that spans C2 over R. Hence C2 is finite-dimensional over R as well.

exr-subspaces-a1.title: A1
exr-subspaces-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a subset U of a vector space V over F to be a subspace.
  2. State the subspace test.
  3. True or false: ∅ is a subspace of every vector space. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if U is a subspace of V and W is a subspace of U, then W is a subspace of V. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: the union of two subspaces is never a subspace. Justify your answer.
  6. Which condition of the subspace test would you check first to show that {(x,y,z)∈R3:x+y+z=1} is not a subspace of R3? Carry out the check.

exr-subspaces-b1.title: B1: Which Are Subspaces?
exr-subspaces-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are subspaces of the given vector space over R. Justify your answer.

  1. {(x,y,z)∈R3:x−2y+z=0} in R3.
  2. {(x,y,z)∈R3:x=y2} in R3.
  3. {A∈M2(R):A is invertible} in M2(R).
  4. {A∈M2(R):a12=2a21} in M2(R).
  5. {p∈R[x]:p(2)=0 and p′(2)=0} in R[x], where p′ is the derivative of p.
  6. The even functions {f∈RR:f(−t)=f(t) for all t∈R} in RR.
  7. {f∈RR:f(0)=1} in RR.
  8. The continuous functions R→R, in RR.

exr-subspaces-b2.title: B2: Matrices Commuting with a Given Matrix
exr-subspaces-b2.title_html: B2: Matrices Commuting with a Given Matrix
exr-subspaces-b2.html:
Fix B∈Mn(F), and let C(B)={A∈Mn(F):AB=BA}.

  1. Prove that C(B) is a subspace of Mn(F).
  2. Let n=2, F=R and B=(1002). Find all A∈C(B). Hence describe C(B) in words.

exr-subspaces-b3.title: B3: Intersection and Union of Two Planes
exr-subspaces-b3.title_html: B3: Intersection and Union of Two Planes
exr-subspaces-b3.html:
In R3, let U={(x,y,z):x+y+z=0} and W={(x,y,z):x−y=0}.

  1. Explain why U and W are subspaces of R3, and find U∩W.
  2. Find u∈U with u∉W and w∈W with w∉U. Hence show directly that U∪W is not a subspace of R3.

exr-subspaces-c1.title: C1: Covering a Space by Subspaces
exr-subspaces-c1.title_html: C1: Covering a Space by Subspaces
exr-subspaces-c1.html:
1. Let V be a vector space over any field F. Prove that V is not the union of two proper subspaces.
  2. Show that F22 is the union of three proper subspaces.

Hint: for (a), use @prp-union-subspaces.

exr-subspaces-c2.title: C2: The Sum of Two Subspaces
exr-subspaces-c2.title_html: C2: The Sum of Two Subspaces
exr-subspaces-c2.html:
Let U and W be subspaces of a vector space V over F, and let U+W={u+w:u∈U, w∈W}.

  1. Prove that U+W is a subspace of V containing both U and W.
  2. Prove that if X is a subspace of V with U∪W⊆X, then U+W⊆X.
  3. For the two axes U and W of @exm-union-axes, show that U+W=R2.

exr-subspaces-c3.title: C3: A One-Line Test, and a Test over \nF_2
exr-subspaces-c3.title_html: C3: A One-Line Test, and a Test over F2
exr-subspaces-c3.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and U⊆V.

  1. Prove that U is a subspace of V if and only if U≠∅ and au+w∈U for all a∈F and u,w∈U.
  2. Suppose F=F2. Prove that U is a subspace of V if and only if 0∈U and U is closed under addition.
  3. Show by an example that the statement in (b) is false over R.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-a1.title: A1
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-a1.html:
1. Define the sum U1+⋯+Uk of subspaces of V, and what it means for the sum to be direct.
  2. State the dimension formula for dim⁡(U+W), with its hypotheses.
  3. True or false: if V=U+W and U∩W={0}, then V=U⊕W. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if U1,U2,U3 are subspaces with Ui∩Uj={0} for all i≠j, then the sum U1+U2+U3 is direct. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if U is a subspace of V with U≠V, then V∖U is a complement of U. Justify your answer.
  6. Name the method used to prove the dimension formula, in four steps.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b1.title: B1: Two Planes in \nR^4
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b1.title_html: B1: Two Planes in R4
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b1.html:
Let U=span((1,2,0,1),(0,1,1,0)) and W=span((1,3,1,1),(0,0,1,1)) in R4.

  1. Show that dim⁡U=dim⁡W=2.
  2. Find U∩W and its dimension.
  3. Hence find dim⁡(U+W) and a basis of U+W.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b2.title: B2: A Plane and a Line
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b2.title_html: B2: A Plane and a Line
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b2.html:
Let U={(x,y,z)∈R3:x−2y+z=0} and L=span((1,0,1)).

  1. Prove that R3=U⊕L.
  2. Write (2,0,4) as u+w with u∈U and w∈L.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b3.title: B3: Direct or Not?
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-b3.html:
Determine which of the following sums are direct. Justify your answer.

  1. span(1,x2)+span(x,x3) in R[x]≤3.
  2. Tup+Tlow in M2(R), where Tup and Tlow are the upper and lower triangular matrices.
  3. span((1,0,0))+span((0,1,0))+span((1,1,1)) in R3.
  4. span((1,1,0))+span((0,1,1))+span((1,0,−1)) in R3.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c1.title: C1: Symmetric Plus Skew over \nF_2
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c1.title_html: C1: Symmetric Plus Skew over F2
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c1.html:
Let U+ and U− be the symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices in M2(F2).

  1. Show that U+=U−.
  2. Deduce that M2(F2)≠U+⊕U−. Which step of @exm-direct-sum-of-matrix fails, and why?

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c2.title: C2: Subspaces That Must Meet
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c2.html:
1. Let V be a vector space of dimension n, and let U, W be subspaces with dim⁡U+dim⁡W>n. Prove that U∩W≠{0}.
  2. Deduce that any two 3-dimensional subspaces of R[x]≤4 contain a common non-zero polynomial.
  3. Give an example showing that (a) fails if “>” is replaced by “=”.

exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c3.title: C3: Three Subspaces
exr-sums-and-direct-sums-c3.html:
1. Let U1,U2,U3 be subspaces of a vector space V. Show that (U1+U2)+U3=U1+U2+U3.
  2. Now let U1,U2,U3 be finite-dimensional. Prove that dim⁡(U1+U2+U3)=dim⁡U1+dim⁡U2+dim⁡U3−dim⁡(U1∩U2)−dim⁡((U1+U2)∩U3).
  3. In R3, let U1={z=0}, U2={y=0} and U3={y=z}. Compute dim⁡(U1+U2+U3), every dim⁡(Ui∩Uj) and dim⁡(U1∩U2∩U3). Show that the inclusion–exclusion formula fails, and compare with (b).

Hint: for (b), apply the dimension formula twice.

exr-vector-spaces-a1.title: A1
exr-vector-spaces-a1.html:
1. State the eight axioms of a vector space over a field F, and say which of them involve scalars.
  2. Identify the zero vector in each of: M2×3(R); R[x]≤2; RR; the space R>0 of @exm-positive-reals.
  3. True or false: a vector space can have exactly two elements. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: in every vector space, v+v=0 implies v=0. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if av=bv and v≠0, then a=b. Justify your answer.

exr-vector-spaces-b1.title: B1: Which Are Vector Spaces?
exr-vector-spaces-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are vector spaces. Justify your answer.

  1. R2 over R, with the usual scalar multiplication but with addition (x,y)+(x′,y′):=(x+x′,0).
  2. The set of upper triangular matrices in M2(R), over R, with the matrix operations.
  3. {p∈R[x]:p(1)=0}, over R, with the operations of R[x].
  4. {p∈R[x]:p(1)=1}, over R, with the operations of R[x].
  5. R2 over C, with c(x,y):=(cx,cy) and the usual addition.

exr-vector-spaces-b2.title: B2: More Rules for Signs
exr-vector-spaces-b2.html:
Let V be a vector space over F, let a,b∈F and u,v∈V. Prove that:

  1. a(−v)=−(av);
  2. (−a)(−v)=av;
  3. a(u−v)=au−av and (a−b)v=av−bv.

Hint: to show a vector equals −(av), use @thm-inverse-unique.

exr-vector-spaces-b3.title: B3: Finishing the Positive Reals
exr-vector-spaces-b3.html:
Let V=R>0 with the operations ⊞ and ⊡ of @exm-positive-reals.

  1. Verify (VS1), (VS2), (VS5) and (VS7). Hence V is a vector space over R.
  2. Compute the vector (2⊡3)⊞((−1)⊡6).
  3. Find the vector −(2⊡3), and check your answer against @thm-negative-scalar-dist.

exr-vector-spaces-c1.title: C1: Commutativity Comes for Free
exr-vector-spaces-c1.html:
Let V be a set with operations +:V×V→V and ⋅:F×V→V satisfying (VS2)–(VS8), but not necessarily (VS1). Fix 0 as in (VS3).

  1. Let v∈V and v′ as in (VS4). Put w=v′+v. Show that w+w=w, and deduce that w=0.
  2. Show that 0+v=v for every v∈V.
  3. Deduce that both cancellation laws hold: u+v=u+w implies v=w, and v+u=w+u implies v=w.
  4. By expanding (1+1)(u+v) in two ways, prove that u+v=v+u for all u,v∈V.

Hint: in (a), add an additive inverse of w on the right. The proof of @thm-left-cancellation used (VS1), so it cannot be quoted in (c).

exr-vector-spaces-c2.title: C2: How Big Is a Vector Space?
exr-vector-spaces-c2.title_html: C2: How Big Is a Vector Space?
exr-vector-spaces-c2.html:
1. Let F be an infinite field and V≠{0} a vector space over F. Prove that V is an infinite set.
  2. Let p be a prime and n≥1. How many elements does the vector space Fpn over Fp have? Explain why this does not contradict (a).

Hint: for (a), fix v≠0 and consider the function F→V, a↦av.

exr-vector-spaces-c3.title: C3: Shrinking the Field
exr-vector-spaces-c3.html:
Let F be a field and let K⊆F be a subset with 0,1∈K that is closed under addition, multiplication, negatives, and inverses of non-zero elements. (So K is itself a field with the operations of F; for example Q⊆R⊆C.)

  1. Let V be a vector space over F. Prove that V, with the same addition and with scalar multiplication restricted to K×V, is a vector space over K.
  2. Deduce that Cn is a vector space over R and over Q.
  3. Explain why R, with its usual addition and multiplication, is not a vector space over C.

lem-append-independent.title: Appending a Vector to an Independent List
lem-append-independent.title_html: Appending a Vector to an Independent List
lem-append-independent.html: Let (u1,…,uk) be a linearly independent list in a vector space V, and let v∈V. Then (u1,…,uk,v) is linearly independent if and only if v∉span(u1,…,uk).

lem-countable-sets.title: Countable Sets
lem-countable-sets.html:
1. If A is countable and f:A→A′ is surjective, then A′ is countable.
  2. N×N is countable.
  3. If A and A′ are countable, then A×A′ is countable.
  4. Q is countable, and Qn is countable for every n≥1.

lem-reals-uncountable.title: \nR Is Uncountable
lem-reals-uncountable.title_html: R Is Uncountable
lem-reals-uncountable.html: Assuming the nested interval property, there is no surjection N→R.

prp-span-basic-properties.title: Basic Properties of Span
prp-span-basic-properties.html:
Let V be a vector space and S,T⊆V.

  1. If T⊆span(S), then span(T)⊆span(S).
  2. (Monotonicity) If T⊆S, then span(T)⊆span(S).
  3. span(span(S))=span(S).

prp-sum-of-spans.title: Sum of Spans
prp-sum-of-spans.html: Let L1,…,Lk be finite lists of vectors in V, and let L be the list obtained by writing L1,…,Lk one after another. Then span(L1)+⋯+span(Lk)=span(L).

prp-union-subspaces.title: Union of Two Subspaces
prp-union-subspaces.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let U and W be subspaces of V. Then U∪W is a subspace of V if and only if U⊆W or W⊆U.

thm-basis-extension.title: Basis Extension Theorem
thm-basis-extension.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space with dim⁡V=n, and let (u1,…,um) be a linearly independent list in V. Then m≤n, and there are vectors vm+1,…,vn∈V such that (u1,…,um,vm+1,…,vn) is a basis of V. Moreover, the v’s can be chosen from any given basis of V.

thm-basis-extension-general.title: Basis Extension, General Form
thm-basis-extension-general.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let S⊆V be a linearly independent subset. Then there is a basis B of V with S⊆B.

thm-basis-theorem.title: Basis Theorem
thm-basis-theorem.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space. Then V has a basis, and any two bases of V have the same length.

thm-complement-exists.title: Existence of Complements
thm-complement-exists.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and U a subspace of V. Then there is a subspace W of V with V=U⊕W. Every such W satisfies dim⁡W=dim⁡V−dim⁡U.

thm-complexification-basis.title: A Real Basis Is a Complex Basis of the Complexification
thm-complexification-basis.title_html: A Real Basis Is a Complex Basis of the Complexification
thm-complexification-basis.html: Let V be a vector space over R with basis (v1,…,vn). Then (v1,…,vn), that is, ((v1,0),…,(vn,0)), is a basis of VC over C. In particular dimC⁡VC=dimR⁡V.

thm-coordinates-linear.title: Coordinates Respect the Operations
thm-coordinates-linear.html: Let B=(v1,…,vn) be a basis of a vector space V over F. Then for all u,v∈V and c∈F, [u+v]B=[u]B+[v]B,[cv]B=c[v]B. Moreover, every column (a1,…,an)∈Fn is the coordinate vector of exactly one vector of V, namely a1v1+⋯+anvn.

thm-dim-impl-eq.title: Equal Dimension Forces Equality
thm-dim-impl-eq.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and U a subspace of V. If dim⁡U=dim⁡V, then U=V.

thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.title: Dimension Formula for Sums
thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim.html: Let U and W be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space V. Then U+W is finite-dimensional, and dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W−dim⁡(U∩W).

thm-direct-sum-criteria.title: Direct Sum Criteria for Two Subspaces
thm-direct-sum-criteria.title_html: Direct Sum Criteria for Two Subspaces
thm-direct-sum-criteria.html:
Let U and W be subspaces of a vector space V. The following are equivalent:

  1. the sum U+W is direct;
  2. U∩W={0}.

If moreover U and W are finite-dimensional, they are also equivalent to

  1. dim⁡(U+W)=dim⁡U+dim⁡W.

thm-direct-sum-k-criteria.title: Direct Sum Criteria for Several Subspaces
thm-direct-sum-k-criteria.title_html: Direct Sum Criteria for Several Subspaces
thm-direct-sum-k-criteria.html:
Let U1,…,Uk be subspaces of a vector space V, and write S=U1+⋯+Uk. The following are equivalent:

  1. the sum S is direct;
  2. the only way to write 0=u1+⋯+uk with ui∈Ui is u1=⋯=uk=0;
  3. for every j=1,…,k, Uj∩∑i≠jUi={0}.

If moreover each Ui is finite-dimensional with a basis Bi, and B is the list obtained by writing B1,…,Bk one after another, then (a)–(c) are also equivalent to

  1. B is a basis of S;
  2. dim⁡S=dim⁡U1+⋯+dim⁡Uk.

thm-distinct-degrees-independent.title: Polynomials of Distinct Degrees Are Independent
thm-distinct-degrees-independent.title_html: Polynomials of Distinct Degrees Are Independent
thm-distinct-degrees-independent.html: Let F be a field and let p1,…,pk∈F[x] be non-zero polynomials whose degrees are pairwise distinct. Then the list (p1,…,pk) is linearly independent.

thm-every-space-has-basis.title: Every Vector Space Has a Basis
thm-every-space-has-basis.title_html: Every Vector Space Has a Basis
thm-every-space-has-basis.html: Every vector space V over a field F has a basis.

thm-independence-unique-combination.title: Independence and Uniqueness of Coefficients
thm-independence-unique-combination.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and (v1,…,vk) a list in V. The following are equivalent:

  1. (v1,…,vk) is linearly independent;
  2. every v∈span(v1,…,vk) has exactly one representation as a linear combination: if a1v1+⋯+akvk=b1v1+⋯+bkvk, then ai=bi for every i.

thm-intersection-subspaces.title: Intersection of Subspaces
thm-intersection-subspaces.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let (Ui)i∈I be a family of subspaces of V with I non-empty. Then ⋂i∈IUi is a subspace of V.

thm-inverse-unique.title: Additive Inverse Is Unique
thm-inverse-unique.html: Let V be a vector space over F and v∈V. There is exactly one v′∈V with v+v′=0.

thm-left-cancellation.title: Left Cancellation Law
thm-left-cancellation.html: Let V be a vector space over F and let u,v,w∈V. If u+v=u+w, then v=w.

thm-linear-dependence-lemma.title: Linear Dependence Lemma
thm-linear-dependence-lemma.html:
Let V be a vector space over F, and let (v1,…,vk) be a linearly dependent list in V. Then:

  1. there is an index j∈{1,…,k} with vj∈span(v1,…,vj−1). For j=1 this means v1=0, so if v1≠0, then j≥2;
  2. for any such j, removing vj does not change the span: span(v1,…,vj−1,vj+1,…,vk)=span(v1,…,vk).

thm-maximal-indep.title: Maximal Independent and Minimal Spanning Lists
thm-maximal-indep.title_html: Maximal Independent and Minimal Spanning Lists
thm-maximal-indep.html:
Let V be a vector space and L=(v1,…,vn) a list in V.

  1. L is a basis of V if and only if L is maximal independent.
  2. L is a basis of V if and only if L is minimal spanning.

thm-negation-scalar.title: Negation as Scalar Multiplication
thm-negation-scalar.html: Let V be a vector space over F. Then (−1)v=−v for every v∈V.

thm-negative-scalar-dist.title: Negative Scalars
thm-negative-scalar-dist.html: Let V be a vector space over F. Then (−a)v=−(av) for every a∈F and v∈V.

thm-polynomials-infinite-dimensional.title: F\lbrack x\rbrack Is Infinite-Dimensional
thm-polynomials-infinite-dimensional.title_html: F[x] Is Infinite-Dimensional
thm-polynomials-infinite-dimensional.html: For every field F, the vector space F[x] is infinite-dimensional.

thm-reals-infinite-dimensional-over-rati.title: \nR Is Infinite-Dimensional over \nQ
thm-reals-infinite-dimensional-over-rati.title_html: R Is Infinite-Dimensional over Q
thm-reals-infinite-dimensional-over-rati.html: The vector space R over Q is not finite-dimensional.

thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension.title: Complex Spaces as Real Spaces
thm-restriction-of-scalars-dimension.html: Let V be a vector space over C with basis (v1,…,vn). Then (v1,iv1,…,vn,ivn) is a basis of V over R. In particular dimR⁡V=2dimC⁡V.

thm-right-cancellation.title: Right Cancellation Law
thm-right-cancellation.html: Let V be a vector space over F and let u,v,w∈V. If v+u=w+u, then v=w.

thm-right-size-basis.title: Count Instead of Check
thm-right-size-basis.html:
Let V be a vector space with dim⁡V=n, and let L=(v1,…,vn) be a list in V of length exactly n.

  1. If L is linearly independent, then L is a basis of V.
  2. If L spans V, then L is a basis of V.

thm-scalar-zero-vector.title: Scalar Multiple of the Zero Vector
thm-scalar-zero-vector.title_html: Scalar Multiple of the Zero Vector
thm-scalar-zero-vector.html: Let V be a vector space over F. Then a0=0 for every a∈F.

thm-sift.title: Sifting Theorem
thm-sift.html: Let (v1,…,vm) be a list in a vector space V, and let Sm be its sifted list. Then Sm is linearly independent and span(Sm)=span(v1,…,vm). In particular, every finite list that spans V contains a sub-list that is a basis of V.

thm-size-bounds.title: Size Bounds
thm-size-bounds.html:
Let V be a vector space over F with dim⁡V=n.

  1. Every linearly independent list in V has length at most n. Hence every list in V of length greater than n is linearly dependent.
  2. Every list that spans V has length at least n. Hence no list of length less than n spans V.

thm-span-absorb.title: Absorbing a Vector into a Span
thm-span-absorb.title_html: Absorbing a Vector into a Span
thm-span-absorb.html: Let V be a vector space, S⊆V and v∈V. If v∈span(S), then span(S∪{v})=span(S). In particular, for a list: if v∈span(v1,…,vk), then span(v1,…,vk,v)=span(v1,…,vk), and the same holds with v inserted at any position of the list.

thm-span-preservation.title: Span Preservation
thm-span-preservation.html: Let V be a vector space and (v1,…,vk) a list in V with k≥1. Then the list is linearly dependent if and only if there is an index j such that span(v1,…,vj−1,vj+1,…,vk)=span(v1,…,vk).

thm-span-subspace.title: Span Is the Smallest Subspace
thm-span-subspace.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and let S⊆V. Then:

  1. span(S) is a subspace of V;
  2. S⊆span(S);
  3. if U is a subspace of V with S⊆U, then span(S)⊆U.

The same holds for the span of a list, which equals the span of the set of its entries.

thm-steinitz.title: Steinitz Exchange Theorem
thm-steinitz.html:
Let V be a vector space over F. Suppose that (u1,…,um) is a linearly independent list in V and that (w1,…,wn) is a list that spans V. Then

  1. m≤n, and
  2. after renumbering w1,…,wn suitably, the list (u1,…,um,wm+1,…,wn) spans V.

thm-subspace-dimension.title: Dimension of a Subspace
thm-subspace-dimension.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and U a subspace of V. Then U is finite-dimensional, and dim⁡U≤dim⁡V.

thm-subspace-sum.title: Sum of Subspaces Theorem
thm-subspace-sum.html: Let U1,…,Uk be subspaces of a vector space V. Then U1+⋯+Uk is a subspace of V that contains each Ui. Moreover, if X is any subspace of V containing every Ui, then U1+⋯+Uk⊆X. In other words, U1+⋯+Uk is the smallest subspace of V containing U1,…,Uk.

thm-subspace-test.title: Subspace Test
thm-subspace-test.html:
Let V be a vector space over F and let U⊆V. Then U is a subspace of V if and only if the following three conditions hold.

  1. 0∈U, where 0 is the zero vector of V.
  2. U is closed under addition: u+w∈U for all u,w∈U.
  3. U is closed under scalar multiplication: au∈U for all a∈F and u∈U.

thm-tower-law.title: Tower Law
thm-tower-law.html: Let K be a subfield of L, and let V be a vector space over L. Suppose (a1,…,am) is a basis of L over K and (v1,…,vn) is a basis of V over L. Then the list of the mn vectors (a1v1,…,amv1,a1v2,…,amv2,…,a1vn,…,amvn) is a basis of V over K. In particular, dimK⁡V=[L:K]⋅dimL⁡V.

thm-unique-representation.title: Unique Representation
thm-unique-representation.html: Let V be a vector space over F, and let B=(v1,…,vn) be a list in V. Then B is a basis of V if and only if every v∈V can be written as v=a1v1+⋯+anvn(a1,…,an∈F) in exactly one way.

thm-zero-product.title: Zero Product Law
thm-zero-product.html: Let V be a vector space over F, let a∈F and v∈V. Then av=0 if and only if a=0 or v=0.

thm-zero-scalar-mult.title: Zero Scalar Gives the Zero Vector
thm-zero-scalar-mult.title_html: Zero Scalar Gives the Zero Vector
thm-zero-scalar-mult.html: Let V be a vector space over F. Then 0v=0 for every v∈V.

thm-zero-unique.title: Zero Vector Is Unique
thm-zero-unique.html: Let V be a vector space over F. There is exactly one element 0∈V satisfying (VS3).

thm-zorn.title: Zorn’s Lemma
thm-zorn.html: Let (P,≤) be a non-empty partially ordered set in which every non-empty chain has an upper bound in P. Then P has a maximal element.
